attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓  Did you select the correct sprite name and tile in the [place sprite on top of random tile] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do 4 Fossil sprites appear on the screen, but only 1 Player sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Reinforce to the ninja that the [repeat] loop causes the code blocks within it to run the specified amount of times in the parameter. Consequently, the loop will run 4 times, causing 4 Fossil sprites to appear. The Player [set sprite to] block is not in the [repeat] loop, so it will only run once.
steps.instructions:
Begin the archeological dig by scattering fossils on the tilemap! 


Open Loops and drag a [repeat] loop into the [on start] container above the Player sprite's [set sprite to] block already there. Keep the parameter set to 4. Then, move the Fossil sprite's [set sprite to] block into the [repeat] loop. 


Add a [place sprite on top of random tile] block inside the [repeat] loop and update the sprite name to (hiddenFossils). Select the brown dirt tile from the dropdown menu.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite around the 4 Fossil sprites on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the [set sprite invisible] block at the end of the [repeat] loop and switch the toggle to <ON>?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the Fossil sprite when it is set to [invisible]?

❓What would happen if you placed the [set sprite invisible] block outside of the [repeat] loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to explore all the options in the [set sprite invisible] drop down menu to consider what different effects do and how they might be used in a project.
steps.instructions:
Make the Fossil sprites appear hidden on the tilemap!


Open Sprites and drag out a [set sprite auto destroy] block. Place the block at the end of the [repeat] loop in the [on start] container.


Update the sprite name to (hiddenFossils) and select [invisible] from the dropdown menu, so that the Fossil sprites appear hidden on the screen. Set the toggle to <ON>.


Click ▶ to see the Fossil sprites disappear when the project begins!

steps.hints: ❓  Did you drag a (value) bubble from the [for element] loop into the [sprite start effect] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How many sprites are in the array of Fossil sprites? How many hints should appear on the screen?

❓What effect might offer the user a subtle hint about each Fossil sprite’s location? How long should each hint stay on the screen for?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [for element] loop runs the code blocks within it for each element in a list. In this example, the array of Fossil sprites is used as the list, which contains 4 sprites. The [for element] loop will run 4 times, creating 4 hints on the screen (using the selected screen effect).
steps.instructions:
Code the project to give a hint about each Fossil sprite’s location!


Open Loops and drag a [for element] loop into the [on game update every ms] loop already in the editor. Then, open Sprites and drag an (array of sprites of kind) value block into the (list) bubble of the [for element] loop. Select Fossil as the sprite kind. This loop will cause something to happen for each of the values in the list, which are the 4 Fossil sprites created by the [repeat] loop.


Drag a [sprite start effect] block into the [for element] loop and drag the (value) bubble to replace the sprite name. Choose an effect that fits this project. Use a short time parameter, such as 100, so the hint doesn’t make the game too easy! 


Click ▶ to watch the sprite effect offer a hint about each Fossil sprite’s location on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the (otherSprite) bubble to set “invisible” <OFF> and “ghost” <ON>?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What is the difference between setting a sprite to acting [invisible] versus [ghost]?

❓ Why might it be helpful to set the Fossil sprite to [ghost], after it has been collected by the Player sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The [invisible] effect, causes a sprite to not be drawn to the screen, making it appear hidden. The [ghost] effect makes it so that the sprite does not trigger overlap events between sprites or wall tiles.
steps.instructions:
Make the fossils appear when the archaeologist digs them up!


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on (Player) overlaps (Fossil)] container already in the editor. Open Controller and drag an <is button pressed> value block into the <true> value of the [if then] conditional. This will check if the A button is being pressed while the Player sprite is overlapping the Fossil sprite.


Then, open Sprites and drag out two [set sprite auto destroy] blocks into the [if then] conditional. Drag the (otherSprite) bubble into each block. Then, change the first block’s parameter to [invisible] <OFF> and the second block’s parameter to [ghost] <ON>. These blocks will make the Fossil sprite appear when the Player sprite overlaps and “digs” it up (by pressing the A button), but not cause any new events to happen once the Fossil sprite has been collected.


Click ▶ to see the Fossil sprites appear on the tilemap when the Player sprite overlaps with it and the A button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a [list add value to end] block into the [if then] conditional and update the value parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What will the [foundFossils] array be used for?

❓ What should happen after the [foundFossils] array contains each of the Fossil sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja will set an empty array so that values are added when the Player sprite collects Fossil sprites. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to think about why nothing new visibly appears after they set the list and add values to it.
steps.instructions:
Create an array to count how many fossils the archaeologist has collected! 


Open Arrays and drag a [set list to] block into the bottom of the [on start] container. Create a new array called “foundFossils”. Then, click (-) two times, so that the list contains an (empty array).


Open Arrays again to drag a [list add value to end] block into the [if then] conditional. Change the (list) variable name to [foundFossils] and drag the (otherSprite) bubble into the value parameter.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a second conditional that checks if the (length of array) (foundFossils) equals the (length of array) of sprites of kind Fossil?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project know when to end the game?

❓ What else might happen once the Player sprite has collected all of the Fossil sprites?

❓ What if you swapped the position of the two (length of array) blocks? Would anything new happen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja think through the logic of the added blocks: if the length of the array of foundFossils (the list which is adding Fossil sprites as they are collected) is equal to the length of array of Fossil sprites (number of total Fossil sprites on the screen), then game over win. In other words, once the Player sprite has collected the number of Fossil sprites on the screen, end the game in a win.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to end once the archaeologist sprite has collected all 4 Fossil sprites.


Drag another [if then] conditional into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container, underneath the existing one. Then, drag a <0 = 0> comparison block into the <true> value of the [if then] conditional.


Drag two (length of array) blocks into the parameters of the <0 = 0> comparison block. In the first [length of array] block, update the variable name to be (foundFossils). Then, open Sprites and drag an (array of sprites of kind) value block into the parameter of the second (length of array) block. Delete (list) as needed, then update the sprite kind to Fossil. 


Drag a [game over] block into the opening of the [if then] conditional, set the toggle to <WIN>. Use a [use effect] block to update the win effect on screen.


Click ▶ to see the game end once the Player sprite has collected all 4 Fossil sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set an appropriate amount of time in the [start countdown] and [pause] code blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the [pause] block affect the rest of the code in the [if then] conditional?

❓ Where else in the project might it be helpful to pause briefly?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The [pause] block can be used to create a break in the code. In this project, it is used so that all 4 Fossil sprites can be seen on the screen, before the game ends.
steps.instructions:
Give the Player sprite a set amount of time to dig up all 4 Fossil sprites!


Add a [start countdown] block to the bottom of the [on start] container. Update the parameter so that the countdown is long enough for the Player sprite to collect all 4 Fossil sprites, but short enough that the game is still challenging.


Open Loops and drag a [pause] block above the [game over] block. Update the parameter so that the project pauses briefly to see all 4 Fossil sprites appear on the screen. 


Click ▶ to see if you can find all 4 Fossil sprites before the timer runs out!

steps.hints: ❓  Does the (join) block contain the correct value bubbles and test input?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the [forever] loop different from the [repeat] and [for element] loops?

❓Does the text appear on the screen how you expected it would? If not, what should you change?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out their project to make sure that the formatting and sequencing in the (join) block reads correctly.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to say how many Fossil sprites have been found out of the total number of Fossil sprites!


Drag a [say] block into the [forever] loop already in the editor. Update the sprite name to (archaeologist) then drag a (join) block into the text parameter and click + to add a third bubble.


Drag (length of array) blocks into the first and last bubbles of the (join) block. In the first (length of array) block, update the variable name to be (foundFossils). Then, open Sprites and drag an (array of sprites of kind) value block into the parameter of the other (length of array) block. Update the sprite kind to Fossil. Then, type “/” in the middle bubble.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite say how many Fossil sprites have been found as the game is played!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add customizations to your project such as splash or dialog, effects, or sound?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions will help people understand how this project works?

❓ What type of screen or sound effects might enhance this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project by adding directions with a dialog box and modifying any screen or sound effects! 


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a for loop to give hints about hidden sprites’ locations on a tilemap!

validationItems.text: Use a repeat loop to place 4 Fossil sprites on the tilemap.
Use a for element loop to make an effect happen for all 4 Fossil sprites.
Use an overlap event to make Fossil sprites appear when they are overlapped by the Player sprite and the A button is pressed.
Use an empty array to count the number of Fossil sprites found.
End the game when all Fossil sprites have been found.
Use a countdown timer and a pause block to control actions in the game.
Create a counter to tell how many Fossil sprites have been found.
Customize the game with project directions and other sound / screen effects.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about repeat and for loops. A loop is a chunk of code that repeats until a specific condition is met. You’ll use what you already know about variables and arrays to create loops that respond to specific conditions. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level #4:

badges.title: Deja Vu
badges.description: Use different types of loops to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: Once More, With Feeling
badges.description: Use a repeat loop to repeat code a given number of times.

badges.title: Yearbook
badges.description: Create and use an array of sprites.

badges.title: Roll Call
badges.description: Use a for element of loop to make something happen to each item in an array.

badges.title: Freeze Tag
badges.description: Use a pause in a project.

badges.title: Button Down
badges.description: Check if a button is being pressed before making something happen in a project.
